title: Lower the hill
hook: Shave a third off the barrier. A third faster?

knows: that reactions need enough energy to get over a barrier (activation energy)
doesNotKnow: that the rate depends exponentially on the barrier, so a modest lowering gives an enormous speed-up

misconception: A catalyst gives a modest boost in proportion to the barrier change, is consumed, or changes where the reaction ends up.
objective: The learner can explain that lowering a barrier from 75 to 50 kJ/mol at 298 K speeds a reaction about 24,000 times, because the share of collisions with enough energy goes as e^(−Ea/RT), and that a catalyst is not used up and does not change the end point.

claims.text: The share of collisions with at least the barrier energy goes as e^(−Ea/RT) (Arrhenius).
claims.source: Arrhenius equation k = A e^(−Ea/RT) (IUPAC Gold Book, 'Arrhenius equation'; Atkins, Physical Chemistry).

claims.text: Lowering the barrier from 75 to 50 kJ/mol at 298 K raises the rate about 24,000 times, assuming the same pre-factor.
claims.source: exp(25,000 / (8.314 × 298)) = exp(10.09) = 24,113, rounded to 24,000. R = 8.314 J/(mol K) (CODATA). Node script; Demo.tsx GAIN.

claims.text: At 298 K, 25 kJ/mol is about 10 times RT, and e¹⁰ is about 22,000.
A catalyst is not used up and does not change where the reaction ends up (the equilibrium).
claims.source: IUPAC Gold Book, 'catalyst': increases the rate without modifying the overall standard Gibbs energy change; recovered unchanged.

claims.text: Stage: the counter is scaled to 1 crossing per second at 75 kJ/mol; the products' level (−20 kJ/mol) is illustrative.
claims.source: Demo.tsx rate(ea) = exp((75 − Ea) kJ/mol / RT).

recall.question: An enzyme lowers a barrier by about 12 kJ/mol at body temperature (RT ≈ 2.6 kJ/mol). The rate goes up about…
recall.why: Rate goes as e^(−Ea/RT): e^(12/2.6) = e^4.6 ≈ 100.
